sources.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, version 5, January 11 2019
sources.locator: Contents pp. v–vi; Section 2.2.1 pp. 56–59; Section 2.2.2 opening through Theorem 2.2.6 p. 59 (not Examples 2.2.7–2.2.10); Section 2.2.3 pp. 62–66 before Exercises; Section 2.5 pp. 81–86 through the end of Theorem 2.5.9; separately Theorem 2.5.11 and its adjacent LIL remark p. 87. PDF page index = printed page + 7.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.1
contents.support: The finite uncorrelated variance identity is expanded inline from published covariance bilinearity in the array theorem.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.3. L2 weak law
contents.support: The constant-mean bounded-variance sequence is the row-law specialization b_n=n.

contents.name: independent and identically distributed / i.i.d. (unnumbered definition)
Example 2.2.5. A high-dimensional cube is almost the boundary of a ball
contents.reason: The geometric shell-volume application is outside this series-and-tail-control page; it adds a high-dimensional geometric interpretation rather than a required proof ingredient.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.6
contents.support: The source treats arbitrary row sums with small total variance; our item explicitly specializes to uncorrelated summands and retains L2 convergence.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.11. Weak law for triangular arrays
contents.support: Its small second-moment sum implies our small variance sum hypothesis.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.12. Weak law of large numbers
Remark: necessity of the tail condition for existence of centering constants
contents.support: The source points to Feller; the full converse is instead read in Roch Note 4 Appendix A and proved locally using symmetrization.

contents.name: Remark: moments of order 1-epsilon under tail control
contents.support: Add inline for 0<epsilon<1 by splitting the layer-cake integral and bounding t P(|X|>t); do not assert nonpositive moments.

contents.name: Example 2.2.15
contents.support: Use its tail calculation and the locally proved necessity; its forward stable-law identity is not a dependency.

contents.name: Example 2.2.16. The St. Petersburg paradox
contents.reason: The n log_2 n normalization is a separate gambling application. The commissioned n-normalized weak law is illustrated by the infinite-mean log-tail example instead; no required theorem is omitted.

contents.name: Example 2.5.1
contents.support: The limsup event has the countable tail-measurable description used in the series convention.

contents.name: Example 2.5.2: convergence of partial sums is a tail event
Example 2.5.2: normalized limsup versus unnormalized limsup
contents.support: Record the finite-change distinction in the definition discussion, with c_n positive and tending to infinity; an unnormalized sign threshold is not in general tail invariant, rather than never tail measurable.

contents.name: Finite permutation, permutable event and exchangeable sigma-field (unnumbered definitions)
contents.reason: Exchangeability is beyond the mutually independent series criteria here; no local proof uses finite-permutation invariance.

contents.name: Theorem 2.5.4. Hewitt-Savage 0-1 law
contents.reason: The stronger exchangeability zero-one law is not needed for convergence events, already handled by the published Kolmogorov tail law.

contents.name: Remark: comparison with Chebyshev inequality
contents.support: Explain that the same variance bound controls all initial sums at once.

contents.name: Theorem 2.5.8. Kolmogorov three-series theorem
contents.support: Only sufficiency is proved at this source location; necessity is proved locally from Varadhan, never the later CLT.

contents.name: 2.5.1 Rates of Convergence — Theorem 2.5.11
contents.support: The logarithmic rate is a specialization of the general normalizer theorem; include its calculation inline there.

contents.name: Remark: law of the iterated logarithm comparison
contents.reason: The LIL is a strictly finer rate theorem outside the commissioned weak-laws and series page and is not needed for the logarithmic sufficient rate.

read_verified.status: Relevant statement and proof passages read; full-text fetch stamp recorded below.

sources.title: S. R. S. Varadhan, Probability Theory, complete graduate course, Chapter 3
sources.locator: Full-course contents p. 3; Chapter 3 Sections 3.2–3.4, printed pp. 54–68, ending at the end of Lemma 3.13 before Section 3.5. PDF page index = printed page - 51.

contents.name: Theorem 3.3
contents.support: First proof establishes L1 convergence as well as probability convergence.

contents.name: Theorem 3.3 — Proof 2
contents.reason: This alternative characteristic-function proof requires later continuity and differentiation results; the first proof establishes the full local claim by truncation.

contents.name: Exercise 3.6
contents.support: The displayed density c/((1+x^2)log(1+x^2)) is nonintegrable at zero, so it cannot be used literally. The same infinite-mean weak-law phenomenon is carried by Roch Example 4.7 with an explicitly normalized survival law.

contents.name: Exercise 3.7
contents.reason: The binomial exponential-tail asymptotic asks for a large-deviation rate via Stirling; it is not required for variance or truncation weak laws.

contents.name: 3.3 Strong Limit Theorems
contents.reason: The section-wide strong-law development belongs to the immediately following strong-laws page; prerequisite BC and extension results are separately accounted for below.

contents.name: Remark 3.1
contents.support: Use the countable infinitely-often event and complement convention.

contents.name: Exercise 3.8
contents.support: Nonnegative series interchange is the monotone-convergence specialization.

contents.name: Exercise 3.9
contents.reason: Borel probability inner regularity is an ingredient of the source extension proof; the established extension theorem already supplies the required product-space construction, so no separate regularity development belongs here.

contents.name: Theorem 3.6
contents.reason: The fourth-moment IID strong law is a special case and alternate proof in the following strong-laws page; this batch proves the independent variance criterion needed there.

contents.name: Theorem 3.9. Levy Theorem — distribution-only implication (i) to (ii)
contents.reason: The convergence-in-law implication uses characteristic-function products and continuity; it belongs with those tools and is not used in the local probability-to-a.s. result.

contents.name: Exercise 3.10
contents.reason: The characteristic-function dilation inequality supports only the deferred distribution implication of Levy theorem, not the independent Cauchy/maximal route.

contents.name: Exercise 3.11
contents.support: Full general Cauchy-in-probability completeness statement, proved with a summable-error subsequence; used in the independent-series equivalence.

contents.name: Exercise 3.12
contents.support: The decreasing tail-oscillation and measurable Cauchy argument is fully included in the convergence criterion.

contents.name: Theorem 3.12 — truncated mean and variance necessity

read_verified.status: Complete scoped proofs read, including the end of Lemma 3.13 on p. 68; full-text fetch stamp recorded below.

sources.title: Sebastien Roch, Notes 4: Laws of large numbers
sources.locator: Section 2 Weak laws and 2.1 Truncation, pp. 2–5 up to Section 3; Appendix A Symmetrization, pp. 9–11 up to Appendix B. The course index identifies this as part of the full two-semester note set.

contents.name: EX 4.7
contents.support: Carry the alpha=1 example explicitly; the family parameter discussion is inline, with the atom at e and exact truncated expectation corrected.

contents.name: LEM 4.18
contents.support: Use an interval carrying probability >=1/2 instead of a median; retain both upper and lower tail comparisons.

contents.name: LEM 4.19
contents.support: Both strict and non-strict largest-summand bounds are scaffolded. The local sign-flip proof corrects the sign in source display (5) and uses exact event probabilities to accommodate atoms.

contents.name: Proof of necessity in THM 4.4
contents.support: Use the fully scaffolded largest-summand comparison, independent product formula and symmetrization tail bounds; retain all hypotheses and prove the converse without limit-distribution machinery.

read_verified.status: Both directions of THM 4.4 and the full Appendix A read; full-text fetch stamp recorded below.

sources.title: Sebastien Roch, Notes 5: More on the a.s. convergence of sums
sources.locator: Sections 1.1–1.3, pp. 1–4 (before Section 1.4); separately Lemma 5.13 with full proof in Section 2.2, p. 8.

contents.name: EX 5.1
contents.support: Retain deterministic harmonic and alternating comparisons inline; do not reproduce the misindexed displayed grouped fraction.

contents.name: THM 5.6
contents.support: The displayed one-sided assumption X_i<=c does not justify the absolute overshoot bound used in the proof. Use |X_i|<=c; our Varadhan stopped-integral proof establishes exactly the bounded-series consequence required, without copying this malformed stronger statement.

contents.name: LEM 5.13 (in 2.2 Proof of LIL in Gaussian case)
contents.locator: p. 8, lemma and full proof only
contents.support: Only this independently useful symmetric maximal lemma is harvested from the LIL section; no Gaussian tail or LIL result is asserted here.

read_verified.status: Scoped series proofs and first-crossing lemma read; full-text fetch stamp recorded below.

pages.independence_rationale: Durrett and Varadhan are separately authored full treatments. Roch supplies a fully read converse route and a symmetric maximal lemma; Roch is supplementary and is not counted as independent of Durrett for the minimum two-treatment requirement.
